title: Living in Vow 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer shares their experience working on a course at Google that aimed to bring mindfulness meditation to engineers, highlighting the enthusiasm and dedication of individuals like Meng who are passionate about promoting meditation in the workplace. This experience has led them to reflect on the significance of Buddhist teachings, particularly the concept of liberation and emptiness, which they see as a powerful reminder of our interconnectedness with others and the world around us. Through their own practice and experiences, they have come to understand that true fulfillment and happiness can only be found by embracing our limitations and humbly surrendering ourselves to spiritual growth.

sentences.text: Did you know that I used to work at Google?
I used to work at Google, and I would go down there every now and then.
We made a course at Google called S.I.Y., Search Inside Yourself.
It was a course on emotional intelligence for Google engineers and others.
They felt they could use more emotional intelligence, and so we used meditation.
It was based on mindfulness meditation.
It was great fun to invent this course and to go down to Google frequently and get to know the place and the people there.
But once we figured out how to do it and trained a bunch of people who could do it, it was very hard for me to go all the way down to Google.
It was far.
I couldn't keep doing it, so I stopped.
But I still maintain a connection, and every once in a while I make a guest appearance.
When a new book comes out, I always call up my friends at Google and say, "Hey, how about I come down?"
They have book talks down there a lot.
So I went down the other day to give a book talk and to have lunch with my friend Meng.
He proudly always says two things about himself.
He says, "I was number 100."
He was the 100th employee of Google, which means he was there from the start.
Which means that he's a millionaire and an interesting person.
And also his job title, it says on his business card, Jolly Good Fellow.
That's what it says, Jolly Good Fellow.
Right underneath there's a tag line, which nobody can deny.
I don't know if it's still the case, but it used to be that you'd go in the front door of Google and there's this big entryway.
On the entryway was a giant wall full of photographs of Meng.
Meng with Al Gore, Meng with Desmond Tutu, Meng with Obama.
There are hundreds of photographs of Meng.
Meng is a goofy-looking guy, very charming and funny.
He's a Chinese guy from Singapore, born and raised in Singapore.
Obviously a genius software engineer who is also a passionate meditator.
His secret plan was to bring meditation to Google and then to the rest of the world.
His goal is world peace, and he's very serious about this.
He thinks it's doable.

If you're a young person sitting around with a bunch of your friends, doodling around, and the next thing you know there's Google, which is all over the world, then you think that you can get world peace.
It would only take maybe a couple of decades, a decade.
So I admire his spirit.
Anyway, I went down there with my new book, Training in Compassion, which I'm going to be reading from tomorrow.
I hope that some of you will stick around.
I'm actually running all over the place like a lunatic, everywhere I can go with my book.
Not because of the book, but because I am convinced that compassion is the best idea that there is.
Since the book is really about compassion, I'm doing more for the book than I ever did before, just because of that.
I had very low expectations at Google, though, because after it was all scheduled, they told me that I was competing with Brandy.
You know Brandy?
Brandy is a pop star.
A very important, I think, pop star.
So I figured nobody will come.
Compassion, pop star.
If you're from Google, what are you going to choose?
So I figured, huh?
The singer, Brandy?
Yeah, the singer.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Right.
That's it.
Exactly the same time that I was giving my talk.
So you know who that is.
You know who that is.
Are you a fan?
Are you a major?
I'm the only one who knows.
No, no.
I know about Brandy.
Right.
She's very important.
She played Cinderella.
What?
She played Cinderella.
Yeah, yeah.
That's right.
In the movie.
That's right.
That's right.
She did.
That's right.
Yeah.
So anyway, a few people came.
The room was pretty full up, which really shocked me.
I was glad that probably Brandy was in the room.
Anyway, Meng arranged a little luncheon, and I went down and had lunch with them first.
What an interesting group of people I had lunch with.
Meng now has written a book about our course, and I think that's the name of the book, Search Inside Yourself.
It became a New York Times bestseller.
Now Meng is all over the place.
Many people, I guess, if you're young and you have an idea about meditation, you go to Meng.
Wherever you are in the world, you know about Meng, and you go to Google and you meet Meng.
So there were all these people there to meet Meng, and it was very interesting to see them.
There was one group from Toronto, young people who were very excited to show me their headband that they were working on.
I put it on and they snapped many pictures of me, so it will be on the internet, no doubt.
It's a headband.
It fits over your ears like glasses and goes across your forehead like this.
It's got sensors in it so you can measure your brain waves.
I think the idea is that it goes along with a software course, like an online course on mindfulness.
You can do the mindfulness exercises and then measure and see how well you're doing.
You can get to the place where, I guess, you can become like a Buddha or something.
So this is a good idea, right?
They were very excited about this.
They were so keyed up because right after our lunch, they were going to go talk to whoever is the Google person who may or may not fund something like this.
Google funds gazillions of projects.
They were so excited.
I don't know.
I should find out what happened.
The thing is that you could either get funded or you could get acquired.
It's not sure which is better.
There were also several young people there who were equally enthusiastic.
Their idea was, and I don't quite know what it was, they were precisely developing...
Everybody was talking about all this stuff and I barely understand what they were talking about.
Also I was so jet-lagged because I had just gotten back from New York the night before.
Anyway, these guys were going to develop some kind of something or other to make all work be practice.
Of course, we know about that, right?

But this was like a brand new thing that they were developing, so that people could go to work with the feeling that this was not just a job for money, that it was actually a course, a way for them to develop themselves spiritually, ethically, and in every other way, which I think is a great idea.
Of course that's exactly our practice.
So they had a lot of things to say and a lot of questions to ask about all this.
I also ran into a guy who had come there from Florida to meet Meng.
Probably all of you knew this, but I didn't know that one of the jobs you can have these days is you can be a keynote speaker.
I mean, most people knew this.
So this guy is a keynote speaker.
That's what he does.
He gives a keynote speech about his life, and it's a very interesting story.
He's 36 years old, and he was an elite Marine Corps officer of some sort.
As he says, "I was a very, very selfish, self-centered person, and I figured out how I could defraud the government."
Somehow he had access to information or something.
He said, "It took me about 20 minutes to defraud the government of many, many thousands of dollars, and I had lots and lots of money."
"And I got caught, and I got locked up in the brig.
I had a five-year sentence.
They threw away the key.
And there I was in the brig."
He said, "Well, somebody sent me some books on Buddhism, so I started reading about meditation and about being a monk and about all these things.
I decided that as long as I couldn't do anything else, that's what I would do."
So he taught himself how to meditate.
He taught himself how to be present 24 hours a day.
He really began to change as a person, and he became quite a different person.
One day, he said, "I was out there.
They let me exercise a little bit.
And I saw a little flower, like I think a clover."
Oh, a clover.
Yeah, that's right.
That's what a clover flower looks like.
Not exactly a spectacular flower, but if you look at it closely, a pretty nice flower.
He said, "I looked at this clover flower, and I realized that I had never been happier in my life.
And here I was in jail for committing a crime, and I was never happier in my life."
So when he got out of jail, he thought at first that he would become a monk.
I think he went to some places where he might have ordained.
But then he decided, no, that would be too easy.
That would be too easy.
He said it would be better to just join the world and take over the world and make the world into a place of compassion and selflessness by being a keynote speaker.
So he goes everywhere.
They hire him to be a keynote speaker, and he talks about his story.
He says, "I went from being selfish and really pretty unhappy to being selfless and really happy."
To make it clear that he's serious about this, he gives away most of what he makes.
You can make a lot of money, I guess, keynote speaking.
It's a pretty lucrative job if you get a lot of work.
He gives away about 80% of what he takes in, and he tells people that.
He's trying to convince everybody.
I guess he also has data.
Everybody has data now.
You can't say anything.
You can't even tell anybody your name without data.
So he has data that shows that companies that are selfless and not selfish do better.
They retain employees, et cetera, et cetera.
He's got a whole thing.
So that's good.
He does this, and I'm sure he'll be successful.
That's why he wanted to meet Meng.
He said, "Meng, you and I are twins.
We do the same thing."
I'm not sure how impressed Meng was, but he was a nice guy.
I enjoyed meeting him.
Anyway, I'm telling you all this because it is so different from the tone and feeling in this book that I'm telling you about.
Living by Vow is a very different feeling.
Now, to be sure, Shohaku is a Soto Zen priest and we, too, are practitioners in the same tradition.
We're, in a way, very much like all these young people I'm mentioning.
We also have a big aspiration to completely change the world and turn the world around until compassion is so compelling to everybody else that nobody could think of any other way of being.
We also want to do that.
We also want other people and ourselves to learn how to be dedicated to the benefit of others.
That is, after all, what it means to live by Vow.
The difference is only that, unlike the young people in Silicon Valley that I've been talking about, we don't have a plan.
We don't have a scheme, and we don't have a product that we're developing.
The only thing that we have is faith.
Faith in the tradition that we've been given, faith in the practice itself, faith in the ability of ourselves and all other human beings to be able to do the practice.
We don't think of the practice as a technique or a tool abstracted from its traditional roots.
We think of it as something that is embodied by these roots.
And we have, just like Shohaku, I know, has, a strong and positive sense of what religious practice at its best can be.
And we love the practice for itself.

And also, I hope that based on this love, we're doing the work that I mentioned yesterday that has to be done: reformatting and reformulating religious life so that it serves us, serves everybody, instead of messing people up as it too often has in the history of the world, in the past and in the present.
We're doing this not with a big strategy or plan, a blueprint for how we're going to go about it.
We're doing this with faith in simple, ongoing, sincere practice, grounded in daily practice.
We trust that.
That's how we're going to do these big, big, big, big things.
What I want to talk to you about this morning is Shohaku's discussion of the verse that we chant first thing in the morning, the verse of the Kesa.
He begins his discussion by quoting from the Postscript to Dogen's Shobogenzo about the Kesa Kudoku, the power or the virtue of the Okesa.
Okesa means the robe, the Buddhist robe, a big one like this or a small one like that.
Dogen, our twelfth, thirteenth century Japanese founder, writes a chapter on this in his great work.
In the Postscript to the chapter he remembers how, when he was in China studying Zen, he was moved to tears.
He burst into tears.
He said the tears soaked his robe the first time that he saw the monks putting their robes on top of their heads and chanting the verse of the Kesa.
The emotional impact of this was so strong on him that he vowed he would bring this practice back to Japan, where it had not existed.
And we're still doing that now, 800 years later.
So this kind of feeling is a very different thing from a strategy or a business plan to save the world with mindfulness.
Now, a business plan or a strategy to save the world with mindfulness is actually very inspiring and very important, and we're all for it.
In fact, many of us here participate in it.
Kurt does this a lot, teaching mindfulness.
Tim does it.
Many others of us.
I do it.
I went to Google.
I believe in this.
It's really, really important.
So it's not that we don't like this, or that we think what we're doing is better.
It is different.
It's not better, but it's different.

Dogen bursting into tears when he sees the monks putting the Kesa on their heads and chanting is a very different set of feelings from the feelings one has going forth with a plan to save the world with mindfulness.
And I think we know that feeling ourselves.
I have burst into tears.
Maybe some of you have burst into tears in the middle of a ceremony or a service, or in sesshin, just walking into a room and seeing people sitting.
It can move you to tears.
The sights and sounds of spiritual practice, of religious life: hearing chanting, seeing people moving carefully in the zendo, seeing people eating oryoki style.
This can be moving to you.

And this is a special set of feelings and powerful inner experiences that is characteristic of the religious life: the sense of gratitude that we feel, the sense of connection to a long past, the sense of awe just in being human that we feel when we chant, when we bow, when we sit, when we meet one another formally in the context of Dharma.
It's not that secular forms of practice don't also have powerful emotional feelings.
Of course they do, beautiful feelings as well.
But somehow there's something else in this feeling of sacredness of the robe as a holy vestment, the feeling of the Buddha on the altar, of candles, of incense.
The power of ritual that pervades our practice is somehow different from the feeling at Google, or in hospital settings, or other places where mindfulness practice is offered.
A very upbeat, very bright feeling, but a different feeling.
Some of the people who do more secular forms of practice maybe don't experience very often these other feelings that I'm talking about here.
Some of them may even feel quite ambivalent about these religious feelings.
Some of them may feel not only ambivalent but quite negative about them, with good reasons, as we were talking about yesterday.
Is there a good reason for people to feel gun shy when it comes to religious feelings and the power of them?
If you read the opening pages of Dogen's writing, Kesa Kudoku, what he says may sound foreign and a bit much even for many of us.

He speaks in absolute terms of the literally miraculous powers of the robe itself: how the robe is something that has been handed down from Buddha, and it's something that should be worshiped and cherished.

He says that it has miraculous powers, and he says how sad it is for someone to be in a situation where they don't even get to see the robe, and how lucky we are, he says, to be born in a time and place where we can put on Buddha's robe, which has been authentically transmitted, he says, from person to person to us.
So maybe if you read that you feel this is a little bit more than I'm feeling about all this.
But maybe, maybe not.
I must say that in all my years at the Zen Center I took all these things for granted.
It was just what we did every day.

It wasn't until we began practicing outside of the Zen Center, in the Everyday Zen groups, that I was really impressed with the power of the process of sewing and receiving and wearing Buddha's robe, and how much it's meant to so many people.
I didn't really expect that.
I just thought, well, we just do this.
But I've been impressed with how transformative it's been for so many people.
It doesn't seem like it would be.
Why would it be?
And yet somehow it has been for almost everyone who's participated in it.
It's a practice to sew and receive and wear Buddha's robe.
Of course, Shohaku, when he writes about this, says yes, that's because the robe is the practice.
It's not just trappings.
We say trappings, it's a good word, but it's not just trappings.
It is the practice.
It is zazen.
It's formless zazen.
If you understand zazen, as we said yesterday, it's not really meditation.
It's not really mindfulness meditation.
That might be the outward form of it, but inwardly, it is Buddha's body.
It is Buddha's robe, which is identical with reality itself at its depth.
Practicing like this, we appreciate the feelings of Jews, Christians, Muslims, other people who have deep religious feelings within their own traditions.
We don't think, oh, what's wrong with them?
We get it, because we have those feelings too.
We know how people feel in their religions about Jesus and about God.
So we are sympathetic and we want to know more, because we have a basis for appreciating and understanding what they feel.
As Shohaku says in his chapter, the robe is all of reality.
And yet it's this little thing that we make by cutting pieces of cloth apart and then sewing them back together again.
It's constantly breaking down and falling apart and needs repair and eventually is unwearable.
But it's all of reality.

Maybe some of you know, I know some of you do, but maybe some don't, that the pattern of the okesa and the rakusu, the way it looks and the way it's designed, comes from rice fields, terraced rice fields, the way you see them in Asia.
If you've ever been in a place where you can look around and see rice fields, it actually looks like that, these strips, not exactly, sort of staggered in just that way.
The story goes that once Buddha looked out and saw the rice fields and said, ah, that would be a really good pattern for our robes.
In the beginning Buddhist monastics didn't wear special kinds of robes, but there was a king who ran up to some mendicant and said, are you a disciple of Buddha?
No.
And he realized, well, how am I going to tell who the disciples are?
So he said to the Buddha, couldn't you make some kind of special identifying robe so that I can tell, and other people can tell, who are your disciples?
And the Buddha said, oh yeah, that's a good idea.
And so he decided on the terraced rice field.
I've always thought this was particularly beautiful.
First of all, it's beautiful that the Buddha did not dream up some esoteric pattern based on the Dharma: okay, it should be like this.
He was just walking along one day.
He opened up his eyes.
He saw these beautiful rice fields.
He was moved by them.
And he said, of course, let's just do this.
What a wonderful way to do things.
I'm really impressed with that.
Also, the fact that it's not an abstract, spiritualized image, but a very natural image, rice fields.
Natural, but also not natural.
Rice fields are not natural.
They're made by people.
If you're in Asia, rice paddies are the fundamental basis of culture.
That's the basis of our human culture.
When you think about it, what is a rice paddy?
It's human beings serving the land, faithfully, taking care of it, and then the land in return graciously yielding to human beings the gifts of the earth to sustain us.
It's a beautiful thing.
A rice field is our relationship.
It's not just nature.
It's our relationship to nature.
It's our humanness and our connection to earth.
And rice fields, but also wheat fields, corn fields.
I was a student in Iowa many years ago, and I remember driving across the prairie where all the corn fields grow, mile after mile after mile under the sky.
I remember walking in the corn fields in the fall.
It's really something.
It's a similar kind of feeling: basic food, the basic bounty of the earth.
In his book, Shohaku quotes from a sutra in the Pali tradition.
One time when the Buddha was a farmer came up to the Buddha, and the Buddha was begging, and the farmer said, as many people would say in a case like that, well, I work for a living.
How come you're walking around expecting me to give you food?
Like what?
I'm a farmer.
What do you do?
And the Buddha said, I'm a farmer too.
And the farmer said, well, you say you're a farmer, but so far I haven't seen you farming.
So what do you mean when you say you're a farmer?
The Buddha said:
*Faith is my seeds.
Practice is the rain that falls down to moisten the seeds.
And wisdom is my yoke and my plow.
Repentance is my plow bar.
Aspiration is the rope that I use to tie the yoke to the ox.
Mindfulness is my plow blade and my digging bar.
I behave prudently.
I am discreet in speech.
I eat moderately.
Truth is my sickle to mow the grass.
Gentleness is untying the yoke from an ox when finished working.
Diligence is my ox which takes me to peacefulness.
And I go forward, forward, I never go back.
Once I'm peaceful, no more anxiety.
That's how I find it.*
And of course, as almost all these stories end in the Pali Canon, hearing this, the farmer immediately became ordained and followed the Buddha.
The Buddha should have been a keynote speaker.
If he were around today, that's what he'd be doing.
So the Buddha was a farmer, and in those days the preponderance of people were farmers.
People lived in cities, but most people were farming.
Not anymore.
It's really amazing how few people are farming, considering how many mouths there are to feed.
It's actually quite stunning.
And certainly farming is not now, as it was then, the basis of our economy.
It's the least of our products, even though without farming, there's nothing.
You really can't eat computers and software at all.
Salt, cooking, doesn't prove it.
So it is, when you think about it, quite stunning that so few people are involved with working at cultivating the land.
This is too bad in a way, but also, it was not easy.
All those generations of people farming, there's a reason why people left their farms and went to the city.
It's very hard work.
Night and day, without time off, people get sick and die from work.
And then there's a storm and you lose everything.
I mean, people died when everybody was agricultural.
So it's not as if we can wish for a return to a Shangri-La of the past.
And also, when people farm here and there in large tracts of land, they were isolated from one another, which caused a lot of strange things to go on.
Now we live in cities.
We influence one another and socialize one another.
We have very abstract jobs, which maybe are better for our health and more interesting.

But on the other hand, when everybody bemoans all the bad things that are happening, one of the most wonderful things that's happening is a return to interest in organic farming and farming in general, food producing, good food, wholesome food, and a lot of young people.
I don't know if there are as many young people interested in high-tech as there are interested in farming, but there are a lot interested in farming and in the land.
So, in the discussion of the verse that we chant, Shohaku talks about the translation of the Japanese words that we translate loosely into English.
He goes into some detail, and there are some interesting things that I want to share with you.
The first line is Dai Sai Gedapuku.
Dai means great.
Great, not in the sense of impressive, but in the sense of large scale.
All-encompassing.
And the word Sai, he says, is an intensifier.
Dai Sai means really, really great: fantastically large and all-inclusive.
He doesn't say much about the word Gedapuku, which I guess means robe of liberation.
Liberation in the sense of Nirvana.
Great robe of liberation, which we translate.
And this is what's moving, right?
You feel it when you put your robe on.
You are putting on the robe of liberation.
And I do feel that way.
When I put on my robe, I feel like there's liberation.
Not simply in wearing the robe.
When I'm wearing my robe, I'm no longer subject to the same kind of suffering that I was before I put it on.
The robe liberates me.
Even if I'm still suffering, it's not the same when I'm wearing Buddhist robes.
The robe does liberate me.
Great robe of liberation.
And the next line is Muso Fukudene.
The usual word for emptiness is Ku.
It's the translation of Shunyata, emptiness.
So actually, this word Muso is a different word.
Muso is a translation of the Sanskrit Anamita.
Anamita is non-anamita, or not anamita.
And anamita is a mark or a sign, in the sense of a perceptual support that registers in our mind so that we can identify something.

In other words, you see a person and actually the physical experience is a bunch of blurs and colors, and you don't know it as a person until the mind fixes a sign on that incoherent set of experiences and says person, floor, ceiling, and so on.
So that's anamita.
Anamita is signless, without a sign, without a perceptual support in that way.
So in other words, it's saying that the robe is an illusion, a projection, without anything.
Whatever it is that makes it appear to be what it is is not what it actually is.
In that sense, it's formless.
Its actual appearance is not the way it seems to appear.
So the sign that identifies the robe as the robe is actually not what the robe is.
When we receive the robe, we also receive instructions on how to take care of it and how to respect it.
Not to just throw it this way or that way, but we take care of it in a special way.
We respect it.
But also, the reason we respect it is because we understand that the actual robe is not the piece of cloth.
The piece of cloth is a support for something that is beyond the apparent robe.
And we're reminded that everything is actually like that.
Everything is Muso.
Everything is Anamita.
Nothing is limited to its perceptual sign.
Because of this, the feeling that we have is that everybody is putting on the robe.
Even people who don't put on the robe are putting on the robe.
Because the robe is the teaching.
The robe is the human body.
The robe is the sacred nature of all that appears in physical reality.
So we understand that there's nobody not wearing this robe.
All living beings are wearing this robe.
And when we appreciate the robe, it's because we know that.
Fukudene is like a field.
It's like a rice field.
Literally, the word means a field of blessings.
A field of virtue, of goodness.
So our translation, Muso Fukudene, field far beyond form and emptiness, is actually not a very good translation.
The robe is being given two names here: the robe of signlessness and the robe of field of blessings.
Two names are given for the robe.
I think in the White Plum lineages, they translate better.
They say formless field of benefaction.
Benefaction is an old-fashioned word meaning blessing.
Their translation is actually better.
And then the next line is Hi bu no nyorai kyō.
Hi means to open up or unfold.
Bu means humble.
And again, our translation is not the best.
We say, wearing Tathagata's teaching.
Nyorai is Tathagata.
Nyorai kyō is Sutra or teaching.
But Hi bu is more literally translated as humbly unfolding.
Humbly unfolding the Buddhist teaching, which is more specific than wearing.
Yesterday I read my post on the Sweeping Zen website, and somebody responded to the post and said, well, the trouble is people who wear the Buddhist robe are so damn arrogant.
And they're arrogant because we want them to be arrogant.
We want them to go around acting and appearing as if they are special enlightened people, transcending everyone else.
We enjoy the illusion that there are some people like that.
That really makes us feel somehow better, that there are some people like that.
But here, it says in the robe chant that you humbly unfold the robe.
The idea of humility is right in the middle of this verse that we must reflect on each and every time we put on the robe.
We unfold the robe with humility.
And kodō shōshūjō is saving sentient beings.
So, unfolding Buddha's robe, we are now saving sentient beings.
When we open up the teachings, when we open up our lives just the way we open up the cloth which is folded.
It's folded on our head.
Now we're going to open it up.
In order to put it on, we have to open it up.
In order to live our lives, we have to open up our lives.
We have to stop keeping them all folded up for safety, and open them up.
Once we open them up, in the process of opening them up, we are saving sentient beings.
Here's a quotation from Shōhaku, and again he's talking about this verse.
*We have to live together with others.
This is the essential point of the Buddhist teaching.
We cannot be peaceful unless all living beings are in peace.
We cannot be happy if we're aware of someone who is not.
When we awaken to this reality the Bodhisattva vows arise naturally.
The vow to save all beings is not a duty or a promise to the Buddha.
The vow does not mean that we are great people and we have to save others like millionaires who give money to the poor.
When we open our eyes to the reality of our lives we simply can't help but share happiness and sadness, pleasure and pain with everyone.
To be peaceful we have to do something for other beings.
Our life unfolds within the Buddha's vow to save all things.*
So again, the verse of the Keśa is just like the Bodhisattva's vow.
The purpose of putting on the robe is to reinforce and affirm and strengthen us in our resolve to live for and with others.
When you put on the robe, it's not just you doing this.
It's not just you now parading around like Mr.
Buddha.
It's not just you, a small North American person in the early 21st century.
No.

It's a dignified disciple of Buddha, in elemental touch with the Earth and with all of time and space, with the formless world that's folded into the world of form that's folded into the robe, which stands for the whole world of form as sacred and unknowable.
No wonder Dogen burst into tears when he saw them chanting and understood that that's what they were saying.
Shohaku closes his discussion of this with a Zen koan that was one of my favorite stories, and I haven't thought about it in years.
It just moved me when he brought it up again.
